meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Aim for the sky and you'll reach the ceiling. Aim for the ceiling and you'll stay on the floor'?
meta.ogDescription: Not sourced to Bill Shankly. Wikiquote dates the attribution to 2013 and points to anonymous late-20th-century versions of the same saying.

answer.label: Not Bill Shankly — an anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: In print anonymously by the late twentieth century; pinned on Shankly from 2013
answer.sourceLine: No book, interview, speech or contemporary report has this line in Bill Shankly’s mouth. Wikiquote lists it under “Disputed” ↗, noting that the attribution to Shankly appears in 2013 — long after his death in 1981 — while very similar sayings circulate anonymously from the late twentieth century.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — no source ties this wording to Shankly, and the saying predates the attribution.

source.excerpt: Aim for the sky and you'll reach the ceiling. Aim for the ceiling and you'll stay on the floor.
trail: Start with the specialist verdict: Wikiquote places this line in the “Disputed” section ↗ of its Shankly page, noting the attribution appears in 2013 and that very similar sayings circulate anonymously from the late twentieth century.
The chronology is the problem. Shankly died on 29 September 1981 ↗, seven years after retiring as Liverpool manager in 1974 — so a first appearance in 2013 is not evidence of anything he said.
The 2013 item Wikiquote points to is a fan opinion piece dated 26 July 2013 ↗: it quotes the saying and credits Shankly, but offers no source for the credit.
Downstream, the quote sites simply repeat it. AZQuotes carries the line under Shankly’s name ↗ with no citation, date or occasion attached — the pattern that keeps unsourced attributions alive.
source.excerptNote: Reproduced as it circulates. There is no fuller original context to show, because no original has been identified.
source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be assessed, because the wording has no identified author or first publication. It is not established as Shankly’s, and the anonymous versions Wikiquote points to are themselves late-twentieth-century and unattributed — so no public-domain claim is made here.

author.name: Bill Shankly
author.kicker: The man the quote gets pinned on
author.heading: Who was Bill Shankly?
author.metaLine: 1913–1981 · Scottish footballer & manager of Liverpool F.C., 1959–1974
author.bio: William “Bill” Shankly was born in the Ayrshire mining village of Glenbuck in 1913, played wing-half for Preston North End, and managed Carlisle United, Grimsby Town, Workington and Huddersfield Town before taking over a Second Division Liverpool in December 1959. Over fifteen seasons he rebuilt the club into an English and European power, retiring in 1974; he died in 1981. He was a genuinely quotable man — blunt, funny, aphoristic — which is precisely why unsourced motivational lines keep migrating onto his name.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest attribution to Shankly documented by Wikiquote: a fan article at Empire of the Kop, 26 July 2013. Wikiquote also cites an anonymous parallel saying in Donal Harrington and Julie Kavanagh, Prayer for Parish Groups: Preparing and Leading Prayer for Group Meetings (1998), 32; the catalogue record linked here is the Saint Mary’s Press US edition of 2000, not the 1998 printing.

misattribution.heading: How it became a Shankly quote
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook magnet-name case: an anonymous motivational proverb acquires a famous, plain-spoken owner, and the aggregators lock it in.

items.why: Wikiquote files the line under “Disputed” ↗ and records the attribution as appearing in 2013, long after Shankly’s death in 1981.
The source Wikiquote cites is an Empire of the Kop opinion piece of 26 July 2013 ↗, which quotes the saying and credits Shankly — with no source of its own.
They reproduce it under Shankly’s name with no citation — the worked example is the AZQuotes entry ↗, which gives no book, date or occasion.
Wikiquote notes that very similar sayings appear anonymously from the late twentieth century, citing a 1998 parish prayer handbook by Donal Harrington and Julie Kavanagh — see the Disputed entry ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody has shown that Bill Shankly ever said it. It is an anonymous modern saying that was handed to him in 2013, and Wikiquote treats it as disputed ↗ for exactly that reason.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Shankly
lead: Shankly is one of sport’s great one-liner machines, and that is the whole problem. A manager with a genuine catalogue of pithy, printable sayings becomes a magnet: any anonymous motivational line with a bit of working-class bite finds a comfortable home under his name, and readers accept it because it sounds exactly like him.

The tell here is chronology. Shankly died in 1981. The attribution surfaces in 2013, in a fan-site opinion piece about Liverpool’s league ambitions — the kind of context where a familiar motivational proverb gets reached for and casually credited to the club’s most quotable figure. Meanwhile the saying itself, in near-identical wording, was already in circulation anonymously in the 1990s.
detailsBody: What would change the verdict: a pre-1981 printing — a newspaper interview, a match programme, a passage in his 1976 autobiography, a broadcast transcript — in which Shankly uses this wording. Nothing of that kind has been produced by the sites that carry the quote.

The sentiment belongs to a long proverbial family about aiming high (“hitch your wagon to a star”, “aim at the sun and your arrow will fly higher”). The sky/ceiling/floor phrasing is a modern member of that family with no identified author.
context.pull: A quotable man is a magnet. Sounding like Shankly is not evidence of being Shankly.
